entries.title: EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
entries.summary: Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece have announced that Rwanda will be used as a deportation centre.
entries.content:
EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda

NewsFeed

EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda

Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece have announced that Rwanda will be used as a deportation centre for migrants who have failed in their bid for asylum. The so-called ‘return hub’ will be ready to accept arrivals in 2027.

Published On 17 Nov 2026

entries.title: Ukraine holds peace talks with US, Europe as conflict escalates
entries.summary: Kushner reports progress towards a deal, but Moscow says it has not agreed to European participation in the next talks.
entries.content:
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said there had been ‘no change in Russia’s position’ as Russia and Ukraine strike major infrastructure.

Ukraine has held new talks with United States and European officials on ending the war with Russia, hours before Kyiv’s mayor reported strikes on two bridges in the capital.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described Monday’s online discussions with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and European representatives as “not easy”. But he said participants had agreed to meet in Berlin with the “Coalition of the Willing”, a group of countries supporting Ukraine, as the US and Europe step up peace talks this week.

“Diplomatic processes are actively underway and we hope that these efforts will not be in vain,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.

He also warned that Ukrainian intelligence indicated Russia was preparing major strikes that night and throughout Tuesday.

Later on Monday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said preliminary reports indicated that the North and South bridges across the Dnipro River had been hit. Air defence units were operating, and Reuters news agency witnesses heard a series of loud explosions.

Ukraine on Monday struck a key bridge and targeted oil refineries in what Russian defence ministry data indicated was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of full-scale war in 2022. The Crimea Bridge was again struck overnight, with nearly 200 drones intercepted near Moscow, according to Telegram statements.

US envoy reports progress, warns of difficult choices

Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, said Washington was making progress towards an agreement in coordination with Russia, Ukraine and Europe.

“Important challenges remain, and a final agreement will require difficult decisions,” he wrote on X.

He said he and Witkoff had also spoken with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov about the next steps. Their discussions included how to arrange direct engagement between Europe and Russia so each could hear the other’s concerns and proposals.

The exchanges followed last week’s talks in Abu Dhabi, where US, Ukrainian and Russian officials met together for the first time in nine months. Those negotiations produced an agreement on a prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the war.

Witkoff and Kushner later met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and said European representatives would join the next round. On Monday, Moscow disputed that assertion.

Europe prepares to join, Moscow withholds agreement

Zelenskyy said representatives from France, Germany, Britain, Italy and Poland had participated fully in Monday’s discussion and would have the same representation in future meetings with Russian negotiators.

Ushakov said Russia had not agreed to expand the talks beyond the existing Russian, Ukrainian and US delegations. No date had been agreed for the next round, he added.

European governments, meanwhile, were preparing their negotiating team while maintaining pressure on Moscow.

Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee welcomed renewed talks and the agreement on EU representation following diplomatic meetings in Abu Dhabi and Dublin last week. But she said, “Russia has clearly not changed its position.”

Speaking ahead of Monday’s meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels, McEntee said 113 new sanctions on Russia were intended to maintain pressure on Moscow “as it intensified attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure during the winter”.

“We are also working to ensure Ukraine has the finance and the military support it needs while advancing Ukraine’s path to EU membership,” she said.

Russia rules out a temporary respite

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia wanted a lasting peace rather than a temporary ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to recover from the damage inflicted by Russian forces.

He said Moscow sought peace lasting “years, even centuries”, adding that negotiations were complex and could take considerable time.

Separately, Trump said he would discuss the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin in China, saying he believed Putin wanted to end the war.

“I think he’s backing down a little bit,” Trump told reporters. “Frankly, I think he’d like to see it finish.”

The planned Berlin meeting would allow Ukraine and its supporters to agree on their next negotiating steps. Russia had yet to accept their proposed representation in the talks that would follow.

entries.title: UK seeks closer ties with EU after Brexit fail
entries.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham says UK lost more than it gained after its divorce from the bloc.
entries.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says UK lost more than it gained after its divorce from the bloc.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the Brexit promise failed to deliver for the United Kingdom and that the country needs to reset its relationship with the European Union to combat growing global isolationism.

During a speech at the Lord Mayor’s Banquet in London on Monday, Burnham compared the outcome of Britain’s divorce from the EU, triggered by a 2016 referendum, to the Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale “The Emperor’s New Clothes”, in which no one is willing to tell the ruler that he is, in fact, naked.

“I do try to say things as I see them,” Burnham said. “And to be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years. The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.”

The remarks come ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday, which Burnham said could deliver “real improvements in people’s everyday lives in areas of the country that have felt neglected for too long”.

Any deal, he said, would have to pass three tests: it would have to be consistent with Labour’s manifesto and red lines, improve the Brexit deal to align with what people voted for in 2016 and pass his Makerfield Test, his benchmark for ensuring real improvements for people in parts of the UK that have long felt neglected.

The meeting is a key step in his pledge to reset relations with the 27-nation bloc a decade after the UK voted to leave and six years after its 2020 departure.

The UK is expected to seal a deal on trading food and drink, and make agreements on energy and emissions and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU.

Burnham said the promise of the pro-Brexit campaign that Britain would “take back control” of its borders, laws and economy had not been delivered. Trade with EU countries has dropped sharply, and estimates of the economic damage range from 4 percent to 8 percent of the UK’s gross domestic product, he said.

Seeking to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil that has made him Britain’s seventh prime minister since 2016, Burnham said the UK was back on the world stage. He argued the country is well positioned to lead in an era of renewed international cooperation because of its experience since 2016.

“Brexit was the first domino to fall in a global move towards more isolationism and protectionism,” he said. “It is exactly what our enemies wanted. Russia wanted disunity within NATO and a weaker Europe.”

Burnham said that he will open a discussion with EU partners on Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc soon after the Brussels summit. His spokesperson Tom Wells said on Monday that “no assumptions are being made” and “the British public will be the boss of any outcome”.

Until the next national election, Burnham remains bound by the pledge of Keir Starmer, whom he replaced as centre-left Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market for goods, services and workers.

Erasing that pledge would reignite a subject that split the country: the 2016 referendum vote was 52 percent in favour of leaving the EU and 48 percent in support of remaining.

entries.title: Ethiopia Moyale clashes disrupt livelihoods as territorial dispute deepens
entries.summary: The country's unresolved Oromia-Somali border dispute fuels renewed violence, displacing thousands.
entries.content:
Ethiopia’s unresolved Oromia-Somali border dispute fuels renewed violence, displacing thousands.

Moyale, Ethiopia – Fighting involving police and armed groups affiliated with Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional administrations has disrupted daily life and trade in the southern Borana Zone, as efforts to resolve a longstanding territorial dispute have yet to produce a lasting settlement.

The violence, which escalated in the border town of Moyale in October, has spread to surrounding areas, including the neighbouring districts of Arero and Wachile, leaving communities insecure and uncertain when normal life will resume.

The disruption has affected livelihoods across several parts of the zone, particularly the livestock trade – a major source of income for rural communities. Residents have reported interruptions to business activities and transport services.

A resident of Moyale town, who asked not to be named for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that people remained fearful as tensions persisted between forces affiliated with the two regional administrations.

The resident said gunfire, especially at night, had heightened personal safety concerns, while violence had restricted movement around the town and made routine activities increasingly difficult. Businesses, people raising livestock and transport operators had also been affected, leaving residents uncertain about when the situation would return to normal.

A territorial dispute reignites violence

According to Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), the latest escalation began on October 18, when Somali regional police clashed with ethnic Oromo militia members following the opening of a Somali regional administration office and the raising of its flag in a disputed locality of Moyale.

The conflict monitor’s East Africa senior analyst, Jalale Getachew Birru, reported that a 13-year-old Oromo girl was killed during the confrontation. However, accounts of how she died differ: some people said she was caught in crossfire, while others claimed she was killed after trying to remove the flag.

Members of the Ethiopian National Defence Force intervened and stopped the initial fighting, according to ACLED. The following day, Oromo residents staged a demonstration against the office opening and the girl’s death, blocking the main road and forcing businesses to close.

Elders and security officials from both sides later agreed to remove the Somali regional flag and suspend the office’s opening. However, the agreement did not prevent further confrontations. ACLED reported that Somali residents also demonstrated against the arrangement on October 20, closing the main road and disrupting transport services.

Fighting escalated again on October 22, when Somali regional police clashed with Oromia regional police and Oromo militia members in several locations in Moyale. ACLED also reported clashes involving Oromo and Somali militias in parts of Arero and Wachile districts.

The violence is rooted in longstanding disagreements over administrative boundaries, political representation and access to land and natural resources. These disputes have repeatedly fuelled tensions between Borana Oromo and Somali communities along the regional border.

Federal government under pressure to intervene

A security official familiar with the situation in Moyale told Al Jazeera that clashes were continuing and that attempts to broker an agreement between representatives of the Oromia and Somali regional administrations had failed. He said resolving the crisis required direct and immediate involvement by the federal government.

The federal government’s role has consequently become a central question in efforts to contain the violence. Although members of the Ethiopian National Defence Force intervened during the initial October 18 confrontation, ACLED documented further clashes involving regional police and militia members from October 22 onwards.

The crisis has also drawn attention beyond Ethiopia’s borders. On November 9, Kenya’s Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi said he had spoken with his Ethiopian counterpart and urged the government in Addis Ababa to help restore stability so that people who had fled into Kenya could return home.

Reporting by Kenya’s The Star newspaper said Mudavadi put the number of Ethiopians who had crossed into Kenya at approximately 40,000 at the time. He said the Ethiopian government had assured Kenya that it would work towards restoring normality.

Unresolved boundaries and political tensions

Cameron Hudson, a political and security analyst and former director for African affairs at the US National Security Council, said the crisis reflected wider challenges facing Ethiopia’s federal system and its management of regional disputes.

Hudson said federal forces were already preoccupied with security challenges elsewhere in the country. He also pointed to a perception among Somali communities that Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and his Prosperity Party favour the Oromo, Abiy’s ethnic group.

Hudson said previous mediation efforts had largely failed because the territorial dispute along the regional border remained unresolved.

The historical background includes a referendum organised on October 24, 2004, to determine the administration of 463 small communities along the Oromia-Somali regional border, according to Ethiopia’s National Election Board.

However, research by Boku Tache, published in a doctoral thesis at the Norwegian University of Life Sciences in 2008, found that the referendum was conducted in Liban and parts of Arero, while the Moyale case remained unresolved.

The research also examined how displacement, competing claims over grazing land and access to traditional resources contributed to tensions between Borana and Somali communities. These historical disputes continue to provide important context for the current confrontation.

Hudson added that successive Ethiopian governments had failed to engage local communities to address the underlying causes of territorial tensions, instead responding after violence had erupted.

The humanitarian consequences have extended beyond Ethiopia. On October 28, the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) said local authorities estimated that up to 50,000 people had crossed into Kenya since October 22 to escape the fighting. The agency said registration and verification were continuing, meaning the figure remained provisional.

Many of those arriving in Kenya were women and children, according to the UNHCR, which identified food, drinking water, emergency shelter, sanitation and healthcare as urgent needs.

For residents in the affected areas, immediate priorities remain the restoration of security and the resumption of livelihoods. With the territorial dispute unresolved and the two regional administrations yet to reach a lasting agreement, uncertainty continues over when affected communities will be able to return to normal life.

“The federal government is ultimately responsible for addressing violence, even along regional borders,” Hudson told Al Jazeera.

entries.title: Paraguay ex-president moved to military jail amid special treatment reports
entries.summary: Santiago Pena has been accused of corruption following the collapse of Ueno Bank earlier this month.
entries.content:
Santiago Pena has been accused of corruption following the collapse of Ueno Bank earlier this month.

Paraguay’s former President Santiago Pena has been transferred to a military prison on a judge’s orders, following reports that he was granted special amenities while awaiting trial for a financial corruption scandal.

On Monday, Judge Osmar Legal ordered Pena to be moved from the Presidential Escort Regiment, a military base in the capital city of Asuncion.

There, media reports indicated he had a large dining room, furnishings, a private gym and a bathroom, sparking public backlash.

His new lodgings are inside Vinas Cue military prison. Pena, however, is to be held separately from the facility’s other prisoners for his safety.

Allegations against the former president are at the centre of a corruption scandal related to the collapse of a major financial lender, Ueno Bank, used by more than half of the country’s adult population.

The political crisis erupted into the public spotlight on November 3, when Paraguay’s central bank took control of Ueno after declaring it insolvent.

In doing so, it froze account activity for nearly three million people. In the months before its collapse, Ueno held roughly $850m in public funds, including money for retirement pensions.

The scandal led to the end of Pena’s presidency. A member of the conservative Colorado Party, a leading force in Paraguay’s politics, Pena saw his political allies distance themselves from him in the wake of the lender’s collapse.

His attempts to resign were rejected, as Paraguay’s Congress instead pursued impeachment proceedings against him. He was removed from office on November 6.

As criminal investigations unfolded, scrutiny fell on Pena’s role as a shareholder in Ueno’s parent company. Pena has denied wrongdoing and said he sold his shares in 2025.

Prosecutors, however, have accused Pena of using his position in office to direct public funds to the bank while it made insider loans to owners.

He faces charges including breach of trust, criminal association and administration for personal gain. Angry protests accompanied Pena’s removal, and he was ordered to be held in pretrial detention.

His former vice president, Pedro Alliana, has since been sworn in to lead Paraguay’s executive branch.

In a news conference on Monday, Alliana said he had dismissed a military official, Colonel Jose David Daiub, accused of giving Pena special treatment while in detention.

“Our priority is to guarantee the country’s stability, restore confidence, and provide concrete and rapid solutions,” said Alliana.

Paraguayans, he added, “deserve to know the truth”. Pena’s transfer to a military prison came on his 48th birthday.

entries.title: EU agrees to resurrect cooperation deal with Syria
entries.summary: Decision aims to bolster bloc's ties with Damascus following the collapse of Assad's government in December 2024.
entries.content:
Decision aims to bolster the bloc’s ties with Damascus following the Assad government’s collapse in December 2024.

European Union foreign ministers have agreed to revive a nearly 20-year-old cooperation deal with Syria, as the bloc presses to strengthen ties with the war-scarred country.

“Syria needs investment and a successful transition,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Monday.

“The aim is to give Europe and Syria a framework for trade, political dialogue and closer cooperation as soon as possible.”

The EU-Syria association agreement was first made in 2008 under then-President Bashar al-Assad, but it was never fully signed by either side, owing to concerns over the Assad government’s human rights record.

Kallas said EU foreign ministers meeting in Brussels had “supported moving ahead” with that deal and launching talks for an updated one.

A discussion paper prepared by the bloc’s diplomatic service ahead of the meeting outlined one of Brussels’ most ambitious efforts yet to normalise ties with Syria, less than two years after Assad’s fall.

Kallas said diplomats would now work through the technical and legal details to finalise the agreement, which would create a framework for free trade, political dialogue and broader cooperation between Brussels and Damascus.

“Everybody said that we need to engage with Syria because if we don’t engage, then this vacuum will be filled by other players,” Kallas said.

Kallas said the EU would set out new conditions for Syria to secure an updated deal.

“We should have clear conditionality regarding human rights,” she said.

“We should have also the nonrecognition of occupied Ukrainian, Georgian territories that they have recognised under Assad’s regime.”

The move is the latest in the 27-nation bloc’s efforts to bolster ties with Damascus and its new leader, President Ahmed al-Sharaa.

The EU in 2025 removed its crushing sanctions on Syria’s economy in a bid to help its recovery after almost 14 years of civil war.

At the start of 2026, Brussels announced a two-year funding package worth 620 million euros ($680m) for the country.

The 53-year-long rule of the Assad family ended on December 8, 2024, after an 11-day offensive that took Syria and the world by surprise.

It also halted a lengthy civil war that left lasting scars on the country and saw some 6.8 million Syrians, about one-third of the population, flee abroad.

More than one million Syrian refugees have already returned home since Assad’s fall, while millions more among the diaspora weigh the decision to do the same and rebuild their lives in their homeland.

entries.title: US Pentagon rejects allegations linking deputy to a Goldman Sachs banker
entries.summary: Pentagon defends Steve Feinberg, amid claims in Bloomberg he encouraged defence contractors to use a specific banker.
entries.content:
The Department of Defense has defended Steve Feinberg amid claims that he encouraged defence contractors to use a specific banker.

The Pentagon has denied reports that Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg pushed defence contractors to work with a specific Goldman Sachs banker with whom he had longstanding ties.

In a statement sent to Al Jazeera on Monday, the Pentagon said the allegations were “baseless”.

“Any claim that the Deputy directed companies to use Goldman Sachs is categorically false. He worked with financial firms across the industry throughout his entire career,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in the statement.

“He has no favorites, and neither does the Department of War.”

The publication Bloomberg first reported the allegations, citing anonymous sources familiar with the matter.

According to Bloomberg’s report, Feinberg guided defence contractors like Lockheed Martin and RTX towards working with Goldman Sachs banker Jim Donovan during their negotiations with the Pentagon.

Donovan and Feinberg reportedly knew each other. Bloomberg said Donovan has previously worked for the investment firm Feinberg co-founded, Cerberus Capital Management, which claims to oversee $70bn in assets.

Bloomberg’s report has raised concerns about a conflict of interest during the lucrative Pentagon negotiations.

Defence contracts are often million, if not billion, dollar deals. Guiding a company that is competing for a contract to work with a specific banker could be seen as a way of rigging the negotiations.

It would also put the banker in line to potentially receive large commissions from the contracts in question.

According to Bloomberg, both RTX and Lockheed Martin hired Donovan after Feinberg’s suggestion.

The Pentagon, however, has accused Bloomberg of seeking to lend credibility to unsubstantiated allegations.

“Despite the Department’s categorical denial, Bloomberg appears more interested in advancing a baseless smear than establishing the facts. Your sources are playing you, and Bloomberg should know better,” Deputy Pentagon Press Secretary Jacob Bliss told Al Jazeera.

“The Deputy is a man of honor and integrity. Unfortunately, some would rather see him fail than succeed.”

Feinberg was nominated by President Donald Trump for his position in one of the Pentagon’s top posts.

The Senate confirmed him in a vote of 59 to 40, and he was sworn in as the 36th deputy defense secretary on March 17, 2025, according to the Pentagon.

Lockheed Martin and RTX, both aerospace and defence companies, have longstanding ties to the Pentagon.

In August, for instance, the Department of Defense announced a multibillion-dollar deal with Lockheed Martin and another defence giant Northrop Grumman to boost production of parts for the Patriot PAC-3 and THAAD missile interceptor systems.

According to Bloomberg’s reporting, Donovan, the banker, was a part of several deals in recent months involving Lockheed Martin and RTX.

They include a $59bn contract with Lockheed Martin for Patriot missiles and two missile contracts worth approximately $45bn with RTX.

It is unclear who the anonymous sources for Bloomberg’s story might be.

Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has opened multiple investigations into leaks of sensitive information and taken steps to limit journalists’ access to military officials and other Pentagon resources.

entries.title: Germany thrash Netherlands to book quarterfinal spot
entries.summary: Jurgen Klopp's side outclasses the Dutch 5-0 in Berlin to secure top spot in UEFA Nations League Group A2.
entries.content:
Jurgen Klopp’s side outclasses the Dutch 5-0 in Berlin to secure the top spot in UEFA Nations League Group A2.

An impressive Germany swept aside off-colour Netherlands 5-0 in Berlin to pip the Dutch to first place in UEFA Nations League Group A2.

Germany needed a win to stand a chance of reaching the quarterfinals, starting the night in third place behind Greece, who had won 1-0 in Germany in September, by virtue of their head-to-head record.

Jurgen Klopp’s side produced a fine attacking display to inflict the heaviest defeat on the Dutch in 67 years, as Xavi Hernandez’s side looked very ragged as they shipped four goals in 17 second-half minutes.

Greece’s win over Serbia left the top three sides level on 11 points, but Germany took the top spot on head-to-head while the Dutch finished second, qualifying for the last eight on goal difference thanks largely to their 7-0 win over Greece on Friday.

After a quiet opening 20 minutes, Kai Havertz headed straight at keeper Bart Verbruggen from a Joshua Kimmich free-kick, while Donyell Malen headed a Cody Gakpo cross from the left of the area over the bar from close range soon after.

Berlin-born Derry Scherhant fired a half-volley against the outside of the Dutch post on 32 minutes after collecting a cross from the right byline, but it turned out to be a range-finder as Scherhant scored his first international goal from a similar position on 44 minutes. After cutting in from the left of the area and working space, he flashed an unstoppable shot past Verbruggen and into the far top corner.

Scherhant almost grabbed his second a minute after the interval as he jinked and bundled his way through on goal on the left of the area only to lash a left-footed effort over the bar with only Verbruggen to beat.

Denzel Dumfries headed over the bar at the other end after running onto a bouncing cross at the back post after ghosting past Scherhant on 48 minutes. Meanwhile, the lively Brajan Gruda came close to a spectacular second at the other end after some neat control and cutting in from the right before flashing a shot past the upright from the edge of the Dutch box.

Soon after, Gakpo tested ter Stegen with a low strike from outside the box, but Germany made him pay as Florian Wirtz doubled the lead with a stunning strike into the top corner from the edge of the D with his left foot on the hour.

Nico Schlotterbeck glanced home a header from Gruda’s curling free-kick from the left within five minutes to make it 3-0, and the fourth arrived soon after as Gruda was allowed to glide into the area on the right and get to the byline before dinking the ball back into the middle for the unmarked Wirtz to lash home his second goal with a volley off the underside of the bar.

Gruda nearly added a goal to his two assists as his rising shot was stopped by Verbruggen after another silky run, but the 22-year-old eventually marked his second cap with his second international goal on 77 minutes when he fired home the rebound after Scherhant’s shot came back off the inside of the post.

It led to Verbruggen calling an impromptu huddle outside his area as the visitors sought to end their misery, and they saw the game out without further alarm.

Germany will be seeded in Friday’s draw for the last eight, which will be contested over two legs in March.
